content: Otalgia, or ear pain, is a common complaint among children, particularly in primary care and emergency settings. The three most frequent causes of otalgia in children are acute otitis media, otitis externa, and otitis media with effusion. However, ear pain is not always directly related to ear disease. It can also result from other conditions, such as impacted teeth, sinus disease, inflamed tonsils, or infections in the nose and pharynx. The specific cause of ear pain can often be identified by analyzing the character, onset, and location of the pain, combined with a thorough physical examination. Otalgia can be classified into two distinct types: primary otalgia and referred otalgia. Primary otalgia originates from pathologies within the ear itself, while referred otalgia arises from conditions outside the ear, with the pain being referred to the ear. The pathophysiology of otalgia involves the highly innervated ear canal, where the skin lining lies directly against the bone without an intervening subcutaneous layer. This anatomical feature makes the area particularly sensitive to even mild pressure, swelling, or inflammation, which can result in immediate and severe pain. Epidemiologically, otalgia is often caused by otitis media, an infectious disease predominantly affecting children. Otitis externa, while less common, is frequently observed in swimmers. Risk factors for otalgia in children include an immature immune system, developmental alterations of the Eustachian tube, and frequent infections. In adults, smoking, alcohol use, and immunosuppression are significant contributors to the risk of otalgia. The natural history, prognosis, and complications of otalgia depend on the underlying disease. Conditions such as acute otitis media, otitis externa, mastoiditis, and cholesteatoma generally have a favorable prognosis if deeper neck structures are not involved. However, if the disease persists for more than six weeks, there is a higher likelihood of progression to chronic forms. Diagnosis of otalgia typically begins with a detailed history and symptom assessment. It is crucial to rule out cancer, especially in cases of unilateral otalgia in adults with a history of tobacco or alcohol use. Physical examination findings vary depending on whether the pain is primary or referred. In primary otalgia, the ear examination is usually abnormal, while in referred otalgia, the ear examination is typically normal. Laboratory investigations can aid in identifying the cause of otalgia. Common tests include a complete blood count, differential white blood cell count, cultures of otorrhea, thyroid function studies (for thyroiditis), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (for temporal arteritis), and throat swabs (for tonsillitis and pharyngitis). Imaging studies are often employed to further evaluate otalgia. A computed tomography (CT) scan is useful for determining the underlying cause of ear pain, particularly when assessing the extent of disease or evaluating temporal bone trauma. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is indicated when there is clinical or audiometric suspicion of a more complex condition. Other imaging modalities, such as radiography, Panorex imaging, and PET scans, may also be utilized in specific cases. Additional diagnostic studies include tympanometry, audiometry, and upper aerodigestive tract endoscopy, which can provide further insights into the underlying pathology. Treatment of otalgia focuses on addressing the underlying pathology, whether it originates within the ear or elsewhere. Antibiotics are used to treat infectious causes such as otitis media, otitis externa, tonsillitis, and pharyngitis. Antivirals may be prescribed for viral causes like herpes zoster oticus, while antifungals are used for conditions such as oral thrush. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are recommended for suspected myalgias or neuralgias. Patients should be re-evaluated after a two-week trial of NSAIDs to assess treatment efficacy. In some cases, non-ear pathologies, such as temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorders or retropharyngeal abscesses, may require specific interventions.
